extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, federal agency staff, AI policy researchers, civil society advocates
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizing and evaluating the Executive Order and OMB draft memorandum on accountable AI, focusing on the required practices, definitions, roles, and gaps for federal agencies and implications for the private sector. Useful for drafting comments, agency implementation plans, or legislative proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandated enforcement of civil rights protections
rubrics_metrics.description: The Executive Order directs federal agencies to enforce civil rights protections to guard against algorithmic discrimination rather than relying on voluntary standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is framed as hard accountability (not voluntary): agencies with enforcement powers are asked to deepen understanding and coordinate to potentially expand the reach of civil rights law across government to address existing harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting by companies developing next-generation AI models
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies developing next-generation AI models must report to the federal government on an ongoing basis to show they meet certain safety, evaluation, and reporting procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting is required under the EO (and tied to red-teaming/testing rules); the memo's procurement guidance could require the same practices from vendors seeking government contracts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions and presumptions of safety- and rights-impacting AI
rubrics_metrics.description: The OMB memo provides definitions of 'safety-impacting' and 'rights-impacting' AI and supplies lists of systems presumed to fall in those categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presumptive list reduces burden on agencies (so they don't need to risk-assess every system from scratch), but systems can be added or removed based on risk assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-use impact assessments (minimum before-use practices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must assess three key areas before a system is put into use: (1) intended purpose and expected benefit; (2) potential risks to a broad range of stakeholder groups; and (3) quality and appropriateness of the data the AI model is built from.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an assessing agency concludes that benefits do not meaningfully outweigh the risks, 'agencies should not use the AI.' Agencies must also assess whether the AI is fit for the task and whether AI is the right solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lifecycle accountability practices (ongoing during use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Required practices during use include human fallback, mitigation of new or emerging risks to rights and safety, ongoing assessment throughout a system’s lifecycle, bias assessment, and consultation and feedback from affected groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OMB requires agencies to stop using an AI system if these practices are not in place and to reconsider use if concerning outcomes (e.g., discrimination) are found through testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to stop or pause systems lacking required safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must stop using an AI system if minimum practices are not in place, and reconsider use when testing reveals harmful outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an enforcement mechanism embedded in the memo: the absence of required safeguards mandates stopping use rather than merely documenting risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment for bias and consultation with affected groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must conduct bias assessments and incorporate consultation and feedback from affected groups as part of AI evaluation and deployment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This positions stakeholders (including workers, communities) to influence design and deployment and aligns with calls for participatory sociotechnical approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expanded AI use-case inventory and annual reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB intends annual reporting as part of an expanded AI use-case inventory to serve as an accountability mechanism for government AI use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The memo did not include reporting details; effectiveness will depend on closing known loopholes, preventing under-reporting, and including test/bias assessment results. Transparency reporting's effectiveness has been challenged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of 'use of AI' includes procurement
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB's phrase 'use of AI' covers both AI developed and used by the federal government and AI procured by the government, allowing procurement rules to enforce similar safeguards on vendors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using the government's purchasing power could shape private-sector development if procurement requirements align with memo provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency coordination and enforcement capacity building
rubrics_metrics.description: The EO directs agencies with enforcement powers to deepen their AI-related capacities, coordinate (e.g., Attorney General convening federal civil rights offices), and develop guidance or additional regulations to protect rights and consumers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementation will require increased regulatory and enforcement capacity across agencies and may prompt new guidance, rulemaking, or enforcement actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Call for federal data privacy protections and agency-level privacy action
rubrics_metrics.description: The EO calls on Congress to pass federal data privacy protections, and directs agencies to protect people’s data privacy to the extent possible without Congressional action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies are told to revisit privacy impact assessments and consider guidance on privacy-enhancing technologies (PETs) such as differential privacy; EO broadens privacy concerns to include inferences and networked privacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generative AI testing via red-teaming (under Defense Production Act)
rubrics_metrics.description: The EO uses the Defense Production Act to require companies to preemptively test generative AI models for specific safety concerns and to perform 'red-teaming' per forthcoming NIST guidance, with documentation reported to the federal government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Red-teaming is required for national defense / critical infrastructure concerns under the DPA; the EO's definitions and size thresholds have been criticized as under-justified and potentially under-inclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple accountability mechanisms for generative AI
rubrics_metrics.description: Generative AI should be governed using a suite of accountability mechanisms (not just red-teaming), including algorithmic impact assessments and public consultation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The OMB memo requires multiple mechanisms (impact assessments, public consultation) and the article argues private companies should similarly apply the full landscape of safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worker protections and labor-focused assessments
rubrics_metrics.description: The EO directs reports and actions on labor-market effects of AI, asks the Secretary of Labor to develop principles and best practices to mitigate harms to workers (covering labor standards and job quality), and encourages agencies to adopt these guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 7.3 directs the DOL to publish guidance for federal contractors on nondiscrimination in hiring involving AI and other technology-based hiring systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum risk-management practices when AI affects employment terms
rubrics_metrics.description: The OMB memo applies minimum risk-management practices where AI is used to determine terms and conditions of employment, requires human remedies in some cases, and mandates consulting affected groups (e.g., workers and unions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These requirements position the federal government to influence workplace AI use and add procedural protections (including human fallback) that might create or change job roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency Chief AI Officer (CAIO) role and agency AI strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Each agency must designate a Chief AI Officer within 60 days; CAIO responsibilities (in OMB memo) include coordinating agency AI use, promoting innovation, and managing risks, and each CAIO must deliver an agency AI strategy within one year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How CAIOs interpret the role (technical vs. sociotechnical/public-interest) will shape implementation priorities; strategies likely require increased headcount and new expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI talent surge and interdisciplinary capacity-building
rubrics_metrics.description: The EO directs OSTP and OMB to create an 'AI talent surge' to recruit needed people into government, emphasizing interdisciplinary sociotechnical expertise (legal, social sciences, computer/data science, domain knowledge) and equity in hiring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementation is constrained by federal hiring challenges; the EO sets short timelines (e.g., 45 days to plan the surge) and signals need for both technical and regulatory/enforcement skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and gaps to address (areas EO/memo do not cover)
rubrics_metrics.description: The EO/Memo omit or defer several issues: a national security carveout will be addressed later; EO does not ban certain harmful practices (e.g., affective computing in law enforcement); it omits environmental impact reporting for large AI systems; it does not bind grant recipients (cities/states) to the same rules; it lacks major new research funding and a sociotechnical research framing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These omissions highlight areas where Congressional action, future agency guidance, or state/local policy could be necessary to close accountability gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for congressional action to enshrine protections
rubrics_metrics.description: The EO and OMB memo are significant but limited: executive actions cannot create new agencies or grant new regulatory powers over private companies and can be undone by future administrations; therefore, Congress needs to act to enshrine protections and accountability in law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The documents serve as a roadmap for legislation; without statutory change, governance remains subject to administrative priorities and leaves gaps in regulating companies.
